blocks.x: You can start out as to give your name first.
Mr. For Goldstock. Where were you born?
I was born in New Orleans.
What section of town is? The exact street address would be good if you remember.
Up on drive between Washington and 6th. That's where I was born.
And do you remember the date of your birth?
Yeah, November the 27th, 1894.
Did your father or mother, anybody play? Anybody in your family play instruments?
Well, my father was a pianist and a songster. Played piano?
Yeah. Did your father play anything?
No. Nothing? No, my father, he was a preacher.
Oh. What denomination, Baptist or Methodist?
Methodist.
Methodist.
Yeah.
And your mother, did she sing hymns? Yeah. And anything else?
Nothing but hymns.
Nothing but hymns. Do you remember any of the ones she sang? No, I don't remember.
But I know she sang quite a bit of hymns. She sang in the union's Bethel's church, quiet.
Did she play piano in the church too?
No, no, she didn't play in the church. She was just at home. Mm-hmm.
What was the first instrument you started on? When did you start music? On drums. Beating on people's steps.
With what?
With chair rounds. And the people used to run me off, off they step and I would go on somebody else's step and tell them they run me off.
What would they do? How would they run you off?
Well, they would get a bucket of water and they'd come to the front door and they'd throw it on me.
You didn't know that bill.
Yeah, I heard somebody that did that there. It'd be terrible in the warm weather already. Yeah, yeah, in the warm weather. In the warm weather.

And then, and then again, I kept on and my mother wanted me to play piano. Because all my brothers and sisters could play. All accepted me. Because she taught. But to me, she tried to teach me but I couldn't go for no piano. I didn't like piano. I used to like a plenty of noise. And so I just dove to drums. Until, until we made up a band. On failure between Howard and Ferrette. I had a boy's house named Richard Taylor. Well, well the band consisted of me, Louis Armstrong, George Washington, and they, Joe Rene. And, and, and, and, and Henry Taylor. Boy, they had a plenty of noise but I never forgot. Is that a brass band? Yeah, brass band. Joe Rene was playing drums too? No, Joe, Joe was trying to play clarinet.
Oh.
Then, Joe hadn't started drums.
Was George Washington the trombone player?
The trombone player.
What did Louis Armstrong play?

He played cornet. Uh huh. And so we all used to rehearsal at this boy's house on Sunday evening. On a Sunday we would meet there and we would have rehearsal, we'd eat, eat, and we would all throw in and we would, would throw in. We'd buy a small keg of beer. At, at that time we could get, get one of them small kegs for a dollar and a quarter. And, and we would have a keg of beer every Sunday for us, you know, after the rehearsal. And so we all, we played, rehearsing, and, on, on, until we commenced and some, playing our horn, you know, pretty good. And then the older musicians, they come around there and they're dancing at us, you know, play. And the first job I played was for the Hulu, Hulu parade. And I was so glad to play that parade to come out, out in the streets, you know, to show myself. You know how boy.
Oh sure. How old were you about?
I was then, I was a boy then around about 15 years old.
And how old were you when you started going to the Taylor Boys house?
Who?
To rehearsal at the Taylor Boys house. You said you went there? Oh yeah. Richard Taylor?
Yeah, Richard Taylor. Well, we all came up together.
Oh, and you were just a kid?
Yeah, we was a kid. We started rehearsing when we was around about 11 years old.
And what did Richard Taylor play and Henry Taylor?

Well, Henry Taylor, he played an alto horn. But Richard Taylor, he was a boy who was crazy for music, and he bought every instrument there was to buy, because he was able to buy them and he liked the music. And today he is a man, and he can't play anything yet. Never did learn. Never did learn. He never did learn.
Should have stopped the one, huh?
Well, he would just change from instrument to instrument, you see, until he just couldn't play it out.
Did you ever try to learn the piano? And your mother had a piano in the home.
Oh yeah. No, I used to sit there, sit to the piano, and the only thing I liked myself was how to play the blues. I played the blues.
Can you still play the blues on the piano?
Oh, I couldn't play them yet, but I know, been so long since I've heard the piano.
What did your father do when he heard you play the blues?
Oh, he had died. He had died. Yeah, my father died when I was young.
Did your mother like it when you played the blues?
Well, she wasn't home.
Uh-huh.
I couldn't play when she wasn't home, you know.
What about your brothers and sisters? Did they play in any orchestras? Uh-uh. Did they ever work professionally as piano players?
No. No, they just could play, you know. And they used to go out to parties and dance, and they just played, you know, among themselves. They didn't play for a fact.
They were all Goldstones, they all had the same. All Goldstones. Full brother and sister. Full brother and sister.
There were ten of us. Full brother and sisters. And they all died out except me. I was on the last Goldstone.
How did you get the name Happy? When did they start that?

Well, when I was a boy, a little kid, I used to always could, I always was a jolly. I used to play in concerts and different things, and I was acting. And so a boy, what he used to be, was he was the one who started to call me happy. And ever since that people called me happy all over the world.
Which boy was this? Was he a musician?
Yeah, he was a piano player. And he was, his name was Tom. Well, he did.
Is that Tom Benton? Did you know Tom Benton, by the way? You introduced me to Tom Benton.

Yeah, I used to play with Tom Benton. Yeah, years ago, me and Tom played together. And so, getting back to the... Is that the telephone? No, no, I didn't hear my ring. Oh. And getting back to the old musicians came to us. Used to come to our rehearsal. Well, they used to come around, and they used to hear us, and they would help us out. And they would help us out. You know, it was a little, like, like, Dick Chambers, Amos Riley. All those old ones, at that time, used to come around. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. You were talking Amos Riley. Well, Amos Riley picked me out to play drum in his orchestra. And that's the first good band I ever played with. And I joined Amos's band. And after I joined the orchestra, well, Amos put me in the brass band, which Amos had the brass band. Here at that time they called it the two-lane band.
Oh, yes, the two-lane band. The brass band. The brass band. Who was in the dance band with him when you played for dancers?
They had me, Amos was playing cornet, and we had Winnie's, Ellie on trombone, Charlie Moore.
Who was he playing?
No, on banjo, and we had Jimmy Johnson. The bass player?
Was he what?
No, no, not Jimmy Johnson. Alex Scott. On bass?
On bass. Did you have a clarinet player?
A clarinet, yeah, but Sam Dutry. Oh, yeah.
Which Sam Dutry is that? The young one?
No, the old man.
The old man.
The old man. The old man. Well, at that time, he had a young Sam, he was a little boy. The old man Sam.
Was that before Blind Freddy played with this band?
Huh?
Were you in there the same time as Blind Freddy?
No.
Never played with them. I just wonder if that was before or after Blind Freddy was with the Tulane band.
Well, that was afterwards.
It was afterwards that Blind Freddy came in.
No, before Blind Freddy.
Before Blind Freddy came in. I forgot about that Zulu parade. Whose band were you playing with the first time you ever?
Ever played? Mm-hmm. Way, way, way. With that little band. The old band waved my head up.
All those kids. Was Armstrong in that too, though?
Well, no, Armstrong was to play, but he didn't play. Armstrong sent somebody else to us.
I wondered, how many bands were the Zulus hired then?
Well, the same as they do now, just that one band. Mm-hmm. And they just got us because of where it was kids, and they paid us anything. You know, we were so glad to be out there.
Mm-hmm.
And they just grabbed us. But I played for the Zulu, man. Yeah. For that Zulu club.
Is that an old club?
Yes, it's an old one. I'll tell you, when I started playing, that's who I played for.
I mean, had they been going before that too long, or were they new then?
No, no, they had been gone some years before that. Oh, I see.
Did you always live uptown? Always did uptown. Did you tell us where you were born? I forget. The street about all of that? Yeah. All right.
Up on Drive between 1 and 6.
And you always lived uptown? Uptown. Uptown all your life. I've always lived.
Just the furthest town I've ever lived in my life.
Who were some of the best bands when you were a boy? Who did you hear? Who were the best drummers you heard when you were a little boy?
When I was a boy, just learning. Little boy.
Yeah, the smallest you can remember, as far back as you can remember. Who were the best drummers in the old days?
Well, the best drummers was Cantrap. And they had another drummer they called Edie Chandler.
Oh yeah. I've heard him.
That was a drummer.
Did he play on the street too, or just on the street? On the street. On the street.
On the street. And Edie Chandler, he couldn't play unless he was half high.
He'd get high, huh?
He'd get high. He was getting high.
Yeah, he'd drink it. Did he always play snare drum or bass drum sometime on the parade? He played snare. Snare.

That's how I'm going to play a snare drum. I used to sing when I was a boy. I used to second line. And I always just said I wanted to play a small drum in the brass band. And I adopted his style. And I adopted how he wascapped and walked. And I'd do the same thing.
Tried to play like him?
Same thing. He did too.
Did he play a lot of roles, or would he play like what? Huh? Did he play a lot of drum rolls, or what style did he play?

Yeah, he played a lot of roles and everything. D.D. Chandler and Cantrell, the drummer and the drum, and the maker, it sounded like it would turn a piece of cloth. Well, see, those fellas used sharp drums. All good. Tuned it up high, you mean, had it up tight or what?
No, sharp.
Well, no, they got drums sharp and they got drums flat.
Are they different sizes?
Yeah, I've got a flat drum right there now. And I have a sharp one. I've got two sharp ones.
That's what I don't know what you mean for sure about sharp. You mean it's a deeper drum? Or do you tune it up, stretch the head up tighter? No, you can tune it up.
Yeah. Up to be sharp.
Tune it up, that's what I thought. Tune it up good and tight.
Tune it up dear. Now, you said that one right behind the lamp there is a flat drum.
Yeah, it ain't no sharp drums.
It won't tune up to sharp one?
No, it ain't going to hold it. Mm-hm. That's right. Tune it up, but it ain't going to hold it.
Would it have the same depth of the shell?
Yeah, I've got my black drum what I use in the fuse. Mm-hm. It's sharp as a race.
Mm-hm. What make drum do you use and what make did you like when you were a boy? What kind of a drum, what make?
Well, I always liked a little Edel snare drum and a Ludwig bass drum.
Was there any certain make like Ludwig or Leedy or Duplex or what make? Yeah, or the Heater. Any of them was good? Yeah, they were good.
A Leedy snare drum, he said, huh? A Ludwig bass drum. And that's for the street? Well, that's for street orchestra too. And what kind of pedals would you use?

Well, at that time, years ago, they used to use them overhead pedals. Well, see, they never had those short pedals out yet. You know, they just had them overhead pedals, or a rod on it about that long, and a ball at it. And the pedal part was made out of wood set on the floor with a spring on it. And then, years, he used to pattern that thing used to hit the bass drum.
Well, what about the cymbals? Were they, how did the cymbal work then?
Well, we had cymbal holders.
They wouldn't be attached to the beat or anything, that long.
What, to the drum?
To the beat up. Did you ever use a cymbal attached to the pedal?
You know? Oh no, it wasn't attached to the pedal.
I have heard of that, I just wondered if you'd have...
It was hooked onto the bass drum and got on the side of the pedal. Well, the pedal had a rod on it with a knob.
Yeah, I've seen those, I know what you mean.
It was till they hit that cymbal.
Yeah, when the cymbals attached to the bass drum.
Yeah, yeah, the cymbals went onto the bass drum.
How big a cymbal did you use in those days?
Well, a cymbal about that big.
About a 10 inch cymbal. Yeah, about 10 inch. What kind of sticks did you use? And what kind of sticks do you like now? Light sticks or heavy sticks? What kind of sticks did you use?
No, no, no, I like medium sticks. That's the 5A sticks.
5A. You know what kind D.D. Chandler used out in the street? Big ones or little ones? What were they like? Same kind. Same kind, about 5A.
Yeah, 5A. That ain't too light and it ain't too heavy.
Who makes it?
Oh, one day.
I guess the Omega, that's just the standard way to grade them.
Yeah, that's the standard number of sticks.
Do you remember old man Contrell, what kind of sticks he used? Same kind. Not real heavy, not the great big heavy ones?
No, no, not the big heavy ones. No, no, not the big heavy ones.
Sometimes in the streets they try to use those great big heavy ones for outdoors. Yeah, but no, no.
You didn't use those? No, I used my same ones like I used in the office too.
Say, I wanted to ask you, how many Happys were there?
There were two Happys. There were three Happys. Three Happys, huh?
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Because Happy was a red boy. And so they ate the change and said, who you talking about, black Happy or red?
Was Red older or younger than you?
Oh, he was just around my age.
About the same age.
And who was the third one?
Bill Mermatis' brother.
And they called him what? Happy. Just Happy.
And which one? There was a Bebe and a Ramis Matthews.
What was it?
Ramis.
Ramis is the one they used to call Happy.
He just died a couple months ago.
Yeah, a couple months ago he just died.
Bill Matthews used to play drums too, didn't he?
Yeah, he was a drummer. He was a good drummer. He was a good drummer. Which all them masters were good drummers.
Were there any other good drummers up here uptown? Did you ever hear of Walder Brundy? Do you remember?
Yeah, I remember Walder Brundy. Well, see, during that time, Walder Brundy, he was up in Cantrell. Cant, Cant, Cant, out of the ground. Well, see, they were real drummers. They could read.
What about, say, John McMurray? Could he read?
John McMurray. John McMurray.
Mac McMurray, I think they called him.
I could talk to him, but I don't remember. I don't remember him.
I don't remember him.
No, no, see, my drummer, again, was Henry Zeno. Yeah, he was a boy talking to him.
Yeah.
Henry Zeno.
Was he one of the very best?
Yeah, he was a good one.
Who did he play with when you heard him? With... Huxley the band.
It was Ellis' band.
Did he ever play with the Eagle band? Do you remember?
Yeah, yeah.
Did you hear the Eagle band? Was it a dance band or street band?
Yeah, yeah, dance band. I heard the Eagle band.
Who had that band?
I believe... Frankie Duesen. That Eagle band.
What did he play at that time?
Who?
Frankie Duesen.
Trambo.
Sly?
Sly.
I thought maybe he played Val.
No, I never did know him to play with. It's the only one, the only one I know played Val Trambo and was... Harnished.
We just saw his wife this afternoon.
They were over there, yes? Yeah, yeah. We had a nice visit and she made a tape too like this. Talk about him.
When did he switch to the sliding trombone, Cornish?
Hmm?
When did Cornish switch to the sliding trombone?
I don't know. I don't know when he switched. I don't know the year or when.
He was playing Val when you first saw him?
Yeah, he was playing Val Trambo.
How old were you when you first saw him? Were you a little boy in short pants or were you grown?
No, I was a big boy. You know, I was about 16 or 15 years old around.
Did you ever work with him? Who Connish? Who Connish? Yeah, yeah. I was a little bit of a play.
What did he play like? Hmm? What did he play like? Was he a routine or was he a good one?
Yeah, yeah. He was a routine, but he could play pretty good.
Could he read some of the parts in the bands too already? Did he use music much on the parades when he played?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. He didn't use it.
I was going to ask about John Veen too. John Veen. Did you know him? I don't remember John Veen. Any other good drummers uptown here?
Well, like Woody Williams. Him.
Woody Williams?
Hmm.
What happened to him?

Oh, he was up in California, up in Nugganuga. You know, you know, Zooty? Oh, Zooty, is that Singleton maybe? Singleton. Zooty Singleton. Zooty Singleton. His uncle was Willie Bontop. Yeah, that's his uncle. Yeah, we know him. What about Black Benny? How was he? Did you hear him? Oh, I used to play with Black Benny too, yeah. Did he play snare drums or was that always bass? What did he do?
Oh, yeah. He played trap, saying he played bass drums too. He was a hell of a bass drum man.
What was good about his bass drum playing? I don't really understand how you play a bass drum. I wanted to get some of that down. What made him good on bass drum? That time.
Perfect time, huh? Perfect time and HL bass drum.
Did he put in more beats than the other people or any fancy beats or anything?
What did he do? The man, the man, the man could put beats on a bass drum and he would come right on in with the band. He didn't get away from the band in making his beats. He used to make them too.

Well, I think, what about the size of the bass drum? Some of the fellows now, I don't blame them for carrying a little tiny bass drum. In the old days, did they ever have a bigger drum to get a deeper tone? How big a drum did they have?
Yeah, they had a couple of old team by 28.
They used to use those kinds.
Pretty heavy to carry, I guess, weren't they? Yeah, yeah, yeah.

They almost heavy, but they carried them. And so, so they changed that in the factory. Now, now, now, they bailing smaller bass drum with a, a bailing tune is a big bass drum, the way they bit him, killing him now.
Oh, back to Black Benny, that's hard to say, tongue-tied. But anyway, would he hit four or two on the bass drum mostly?
Hmm?
Would he hit four-four or two-four or what on the bass drum? Or six-eight or what?
No, he would. It's the piece he played. He would mostly play two beats to a measure.
What would he do with a cymbal on those beats?
That cymbal he would use, use that as an after beat, see? I got the beat in that. See, see.
Did he ever use a little cymbal or just a wire beater?
A wire beater.
He used a wire beater. Yeah. Did you see anybody when you were a boy, did they use the two cymbals, so they have two cymbals coming together up there?
Yeah, you know who that was? Clay Giles. Clay Giles.
You heard him talk about that.
I heard him, didn't you? I know I was with Giles. Oh, he used to play with the excelsior band. He had a great egg pastry. I thought he could play it too.

And say a guy like Black Benny, he would come down on one and two with his bass drum, with his beater. When would he put in a double rap or something like that? Would there be any special place in the piece?
No, he didn't pick no special place whenever he would catch him. He's where he could fill in. In some double raps, then he'd put them in. That's the way I do. Right now.
Well, those spaces, do they usually come at the end of a chorus or the middle of a chorus? No, the end of the middle. Right when the trumpets finish playing something, huh?
Right in all the little phrases, between each little phrases.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. On the trumpets. Between the phrases on the trumpet lead. Yeah. So that you fill out the music is the idea. Yeah. Yeah, that's right. You don't want to have a lot of nothing there.
No, not nothing. You fill in the words. That's what you would call improvising. Mm-hmm.
See? Did the guys improvise on the drums when you were a kid, or were they strictly reading?

Well, they used to improvise their whole life, because me, I used to improvise my canard. Mm-hmm. And then again, after I stayed with Amos Riley a long time, and that man broke up, I went, I went and played with the Golden Laith Band, Jesse Jackson. I stayed there.
What did Jesse Jackson play?
He played banjo. Mm-hmm. So that was a string orchestra, dance band.
Dance band. We're just about out of tape here now.
And I still did.
Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
